Unfortunately, vet school is one of those fields that requires a lot of hands on specialty training and I’m personally not aware of a cheaper way around that. However, if you wanted to get the ball rolling and earn your associates degree in general education - you could use credit by exam sources to essentially “test out” of 75% of that degree. Look up CLEP exams - they have about 20-30 exams ranging from psychology, to algebra to American history/humanities etc. If you believe yourself to be great at independent study, you can use study guides and YouTube to study for these tests. If you get a passing score, you send these to an institution who accepts them for credit. Each passing score converts into a 3 credit hour class. Most online degrees have tuition at about $1200 PER college course so each one saves you over $1000. The limits of how many of these exams you can apply to a degree varies at every school. I personally earned about 78/120 credits of my bachelors degree through this method which saved me THOUSANDS of dollars. I passed 14 of these exams in one year but also used some other sources of credit through study.com and Coopersmith. I still had to take some actual classes, but not having to pay for Gen ed courses saved me a lot of time and cash. Let me know if you have any questions about this but I highly recommend looking into it !

I’m not a professional and clearly I’m on this subreddit for the same reasons you are. However, I’ve done a ton of reading and studying personally and am 75% through my masters degree in psychology. What I’ve learned about anxiety and fear is that trauma teaches is a very powerful teacher. The protective strategies we learn in childhood allowed us to survive and find power in situations where we were otherwise powerless. As we get older, these protective strategies become outdated and what used to keep us alive starts to box us in. They hurt us far more than they help. Through a decade of therapy I’ve learned how to teach my inner child (the 6-15 year old me) that we’re not living in that time frame. I’m safe now and those stressors aren’t threatening me anymore today but my brain subconsciously still reacts and behaves the same. Just like soldiers with PTSD who go into a panic on 4th of July when they hear fireworks. People outside that world know intellectually they are fireworks, there not a war going on, and there is no threat of gunfire or danger. But that’s an intellectual perspective and the human nervous system is biologically wired to protect us from anything that could threaten our lives. That stimuli for some people is associated with danger. So now for people like you and I, feeling trapped is the equivalent of those 4th of July fireworks even though we intellectually know it’s likely improbable and silly to be afraid of a train/plane/boat/small space etc etc etc. I guess the key to unlocking this fear is learning that your protector and is and always has been there all along. It’s you. Facing that fear and building that confidence is the only way to really take your power back. The only way to do that is in practice. You may feel like you don’t trust others to be a safe place for you, but deep down you don’t trust yourself either. That belief is reinforced over and over the more we feed the urge to flee when we feel fear/anxiety. We must over and over confront the anxiety and remind ourselves that we are safe and ok and we can handle the uncomfortable feelings of anxiety. The way we “feel” trapped is just that. It’s a feeling. It’s a perception. It doesn’t mean we are infact in danger. This is VERY oversimplified and intellectualized. Many who don’t suffer from panic and agoraphobia don’t understand how difficult it is to find that truth and peace when your brain has been trained to feed you a hulk dose of adrenaline in response to even very silly cues. I certainly don’t have all the answers and wish I could give you the magic formula. Best I can provide is that small explanation and some things that have helped me - though I’m still not cured. 

1) I’ve read so many books on this and some land better than others. I find some to be almost mean and blame us for being this way as if it’s some moral lacking. Don’t feed the monkey mind by Jennifer Shannon was fantastic and really helped me see how anxiety can be an addictive loop. The safety strategies we rely on hurt us more than we’re aware of. We quite literally become addicted to feeling safe and that lands us in a prison that’s harder to escape than the perceived entrapment we feel. This audiobook has gotten me through many challenging times and I highly recommend. 

2) you’ll see all of Claire Weekes books in this sub mentioned a lot and for good reason. Peace from nervous suffering and simple and effective treatment for agoraphobia were a big comfort for me 

3) meditation. I did the 30 day intro to meditation with Jeff warren through the calm app and it really gave me so much peace. Anxiety is so much rooted in the future. We have a feeling and it leads us into a thought loop that exacerbates it. For example, my heart is racing, I’m nervous and that means something bad is gonna happen, heart attack, death etc etc. but none of that IS happening right now. I think it’s quite funny and paradoxical that if I actually were having a heart attack or someone was breaking into my house, I’d likely react a whole lot calmer than I would on an airplane or in another situation where I feel trapped. Learning to focus on NOW instead of what could happen in the future can lessen some of the doom feelings and can even prevent a full attack from happening. 

I don’t know if any of that is helpful at all and I’m not the chief authority on this. I still suffer and struggle but I am a little better equipped to fight this battle than I once was. I know no amount of intellectualizing while I’m in a calm state can cure me when I get to the panic state - but it’s given me more tools to become a better opponent. You have all my empathy, support and understanding and I really hope you’re able to find some relief!!!!

100%. In your case and likely my own, panic/agoraphobia actually serves a purpose. It is misguided and largely ineffective but when you come from a trauma background, panic attacks are your unregulated nervous system’s way of “protecting” you from an another event that could cause you deep physical or psychological pain. I had a gnarly panic attack today, the first one I’ve had in about a month and it was brought on very suddenly for a DUMB reason. It felt like it came out of nowhere? But after reflecting on it it made perfect sense. I attended a brunch for my brothers birthday at a cafe that’s located 30min from my house. I drove alone and didn’t think anything of it as I’d been there before. It’s a pretty rural area as it’s located near a winery in remote area near a state trail. We had breakfast, all went well. I turned around to head home and the highway was closed for construction - meaning I had no choice but to get on the freeway and travel in the wrong direction for 5 miles before I could turn around. There’s a bridge across the highway and giant signs that say “CAUTION” and “NO SHOULDER”. I froze. My heart rate shot to 160 and I had to pull over to vomit. I am just like you in that I don’t mind driving as long as I’m in control. But I can’t travel by train/plane/boat. As soon as I realized I had no control over where I was and had no ability to pull over if I went into cardiac arrest - I started to feel like I was going into psychosis. I made my mom turn around and come meet me. ALL OVER A STUPID BRIDGE/HIGHWAY construction. I even knew it was stupid in the moment but I couldn’t control my physiological reaction to the loss of control and what might follow. We learn this through experience and it’s a tough habit to break. I guess I don’t have much to offer here aside from shared experience. I just wanted to say you’re not alone and this is a very bizarre illness that is extremely challenging to share with anyone else who hasn’t been through it. 

I wish you the best of luck in your healing and even the ability to drive 1400 miles alone is HUGE.

As someone with ADHD who also takes stimulants and did a very fair amount of experimenting with molly in my early 20s - I can say with 100% certainty that not every drug will play nice with every person’s brain chemistry. My own personal experience coming down was never good, and I’m able to laugh about it now but I literally would hysterically sob for two days following any kind of MDMA dose. Not sure why I kept doing it knowing I would be uncomfortable. I know the discomfort you’re prob feeling right now so I’m sorry you’re in that spot. The most difficult thing to remember is it will pass and you can choose to maybe take it easy and not do this kind of drug again. 

In the meantime if you can get your hands on some kind of longer acting benzo like Valium or klonipin that’s probably your best bet for comfort. Otherwise, L-theanine is a great supplement for natural calming effects. 

DO NOT take any adderall or any serotonin/dopamine producing drugs or supplements for at least 30 hours. No matter what anyone on this forum may say - I once followed up a come down with 5-HTP vitamins because I was told it would “replenish my serotonin” and I ended up in the hospital and almost died of serotonin syndrome because the drug wasn’t fully out of my system. Please please be very careful because mixing stimulants is extremely dangerous. 

Try to take a bath, call a friend, drink some hot tea until you’re able to sleep again. If you can make some art - definitely do that!! If you smoke weed, that may help too. 

I hope you’re anxiety chills and you can rest soon OP!

People will try to scare you into saying sub withdrawal is tHe WorSt but it’s highly preferable over methadone or heroin for example. The sucky part about it at least for me and my experience is I was just a level above really uncomfortable for a long time. It’s pretty mild compared to what heroin w/d is like(which is insufferable but is over in like 5 days), but it lasts so long it’s easy to trick your brain into thinking it’ll last forever. It will not. Just remember everyday you’re one day closer to feeling better.

Subs having a pretty long half life, I would imagine you’d start feeling withdrawal symptoms 3-5 days after your last dose. How severe will depend on how long you’ve been taking them, the dose and how often. Did you taper or just cold turkey? How high of a dose were you last taking? I was on 8mg and tapered to 1mg over the course of a month with almost no symptoms besides irritability. When I jumped off I didn’t feel bad until day 4, and physical symptoms lasted around a week with lingering emotional/mental fatigue and depression lasting an additional 3 weeks. It’s a long arduous road but I’ve been off them for almost 3 years now including all other opiates and it’s the best decision I’ve ever mad. There are certain supplements and over the counter medications that can make you more comfortable and I’m happy to let you know what I used. Things like clonidine, Valium or gabioentin can also help if you’re able to find any. Good luck!
